summary: Children aged 6–11 build the dual idea that offspring resemble their parents yet are not identical, through direct side-by-side comparison. The core task is matching young to the correct parent using named shared features (coat pattern, ear shape, petal colour), then immediately spotting at least one way the young differs. Plants are used alongside animals so resemblance is seen as general, and a sibling line-up makes within-group variation visible. Keep it observational and mechanism-free at the younger end — describe features as 'coming from the parent' rather than naming genetics — and introduce the word 'inherited' and the link to variation feeding survival advantage only toward Year 6.
misconceptions: Thinking offspring are identical copies / clones of a parent, missing the 'vary and are not identical' half.
Believing a baby resembles ONLY one parent (all mum or all dad) rather than a mix, and can't vary from both.
Assuming resemblance applies to animals but not plants.
Expecting babies to look like miniature adults in every species (missing that some young look very different, e.g. caterpillar/tadpole — resemblance emerges by adulthood).
Attributing resemblance to the environment ('they look alike because they live together') rather than inheritance.
Thinking differences between siblings mean they aren't really 'the same kind'.

activities.title: Match the family yard
steps: Match a jumbled pen of young (foals, puppies, and a plant lane of young plants grown from the parents' seeds) to the parent each one most resembles by dragging or placing them.

When you place a young correctly, name the shared feature you used as evidence (e.g. 'same coat pattern', 'same petal colour'); across the whole set, try to name at least three different shared features (such as eye colour, petal colour, fur type).
Right after each correct match, tap or state ONE way that young differs from its parent (a white paw, a different patch of colour, a different tail shape).
Look at a line-up of five puppies from the same mum and dad and point out how each one is a little different from the others.
Do the same for the plant lane: match young plants that have grown true leaves or flowers to the parent plant by flower colour or leaf shape, then name a difference.
activities.insight: Offspring are like their parents (so you can tell whose young it is from shared features that came from the parent) but not identical copies — and siblings vary from each other too. This holds for plants as well as animals.

activities.title: Tap-to-reveal family portrait
steps: Look at a parent-and-young portrait (e.g. a mare and foal, or a parent plant and a young plant grown from its seed) and tap a feature on the young.
See the matching feature light up on the parent, and read that it is a feature the young got from its parent.
Tap across a litter or seedling group to see each one flagged as a little different — 'variation'.
Say in your own words which features are shared and which are individual differences.
activities.insight: Shared features connect young to parent, while flagged differences show the young is not a perfect copy — a clean reference view of resemblance-with-variation.

activities.title: Check: like but not identical
steps: Match babies to parents and explain the feature that justified each match.
Answer whether siblings from the same parents are identical or varying, and give a reason.
Find the 'odd one out' difference within a litter or seedling group.

Respond to a reasoning prompt: a puppy has its mother's floppy ears and brown fur, but a differently shaped tail and a white patch she lacks — are the puppy and its mum exactly the same, or not, and why?
activities.insight: A child who holds the idea can name both the inherited similarities and the individual differences, and (toward Year 6) explain that young animals, and plants grown from seed, usually get a mix of features from two parents rather than being a copy of one.

checkQuestion: A puppy has floppy ears and brown fur just like its mother — but its tail is a different shape and it has a white patch she doesn't have. Are the puppy and its mum exactly the same, or not? Explain why a puppy looks like its parents but isn't a perfect copy.
checkAnswer: The puppy resembles its parents because it inherits features from them (floppy ears, brown fur), but it isn't identical — it inherits a mix from both parents and has its own variations (tail shape, white patch), so offspring are similar to parents but not exact copies.
